interactive.title: One arrow, two names
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the complex plane from the earlier lessons, real across and j up. An arrow runs from 0 to a tip you can drag into any quarter, and two readouts name it two ways: a + jb, its parts, and r∠θ, its length and angle. Under the arrow, its across part and its up part are drawn faintly as the two short sides of a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as the longest side, so by Pythagoras its length is r = √(a² + b²). The angle θ is an arc from the positive real axis round to the arrow, anticlockwise counting as positive. A dashed ghost arrow points where a calculator's tan⁻¹(b ÷ a) says, and it carries the number b ÷ a (on the j axis, where a is 0, there is no such number and no ghost). The calculator sees only that number, which is the same for an arrow and for that arrow turned half round, as you see when you drag the tip half a turn round and the number stays put, and it always answers with an angle between −90° and 90°, pointing into the right-hand half. So in the right-hand quarters the ghost lies on the arrow, and in the left-hand quarters it points exactly the opposite way, with a second arc of 180° drawn to turn it back onto the arrow. A reverse switch runs it the other way: set r and θ, and the arrow's shadows on the two axes read a = r cos θ across and b = r sin θ up, as with Trigonometry's arrow and its shadows. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? replays the arrow, the triangle and the ghost for it.
interactive.ignores: The tip snaps to whole steps so the parts can be counted, but a and b can be any numbers, and the rules work the same for them; only 0 itself has length 0 and no angle at all. Angles are rounded to two decimal places and lengths and parts to at most three, so converting back can be out in the last place. Angles are in degrees; calculators and college texts also use radians, where 180° is π, and the rules are the same. College texts also write r∠θ as an exponential, which names the same arrow; lesson 6 names it.

explain.text:
Read a complex number as an arrow from 0, as in the earlier lessons. There are two ways to say where an arrow goes. You can give its parts, across and up, as a + jb. Or you can give how long it is and which way it points: its length r and its angle θ, written r∠θ. Both name the same arrow. Adding is easiest with the parts, and multiplying and dividing are easiest with the length and the angle,[^1] which is why the next lesson needs this one, and why later lessons write AC currents this way.

Take 3 + j4: 3 across and 4 up. The across part, the up part and the arrow make a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as the longest side, so Pythagoras gives its length: √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. That is the 5 you met in the conjugate lesson. The up side is 4 long, the size of the j part, so square 4, not j4. (j4)² is −16, and √(9 − 16) = √−7 is not a length at all. The length is the distance of the tip from 0. It is called the [[modulus]], or magnitude, and it is never negative.[^2] For any arrow, r = √(a² + b²).

The angle is measured from the positive real axis round to the arrow,[^3] anticlockwise counting as positive, and it is called the [[argument]]. In the triangle the up side is opposite the angle and the across side is next to it, so tan θ = 4 ÷ 3, and θ = tan⁻¹(4 ÷ 3) = 53.13°. So 3 + j4 = 5∠53.13°, which is [[polar form]].[^4] Now take −3 − j4, the same arrow turned half round. Its b ÷ a is −4 ÷ −3, which is 4 ÷ 3 again, so the calculator says 53.13° again: the picture's dashed ghost arrow, pointing up and right. The calculator sees only that one number, and the two minus signs have cancelled before it looks, so it cannot tell the two arrows apart. Like sin⁻¹ in Trigonometry lesson 3, tan⁻¹ gives only one angle, between −90° and 90°, pointing into the right-hand half of the plane. So whenever a is negative and the arrow points into a left-hand quarter, the calculator's answer points exactly the wrong way, half a turn out, and turning it 180° fixes it. Either half turn lands it on the arrow; turning it back towards 0° keeps the angle in the usual range below. −3 − j4 points down, so take 180° away: 53.13° − 180° = −126.87°. For −3 + j4 the calculator says −53.13°, which is the direction of 3 − j4, again the arrow turned half round. This arrow points up, so add 180°: 126.87°. That is why you sketch the arrow first and check that the angle lands in the same quarter.[^5] Adding or taking away 360°, a whole turn, leaves an arrow pointing the same way, so −126.87° and 233.13° name the same arrow. Textbooks add that the usual choice is an angle more than −180° and up to 180° (in radians, −π < θ ≤ π),[^6] which college texts call the principal argument.[^7]

Going back is easier. The across part is the arrow's shadow on the real axis and the up part its shadow on the j axis, as with Trigonometry's arrow and its shadows, so a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ.[^8] So r∠θ = r cos θ + j r sin θ, which books also write r(cos θ + j sin θ). 10∠30° is 10 × 0.866 = 8.66 across and 10 × 0.5 = 5 up, so it is 8.66 + j5. No fix is needed this way round, because cos and sin come out negative by themselves in the quarters where the shadow points left or down, as you saw on Trigonometry's circle: 10∠150° is −8.66 + j5. This is how college writes AC. A phasor is a complex number that represents “the magnitude and phase of a voltage or a current”,[^9] the turning arrows of Trigonometry lessons 6 and 7: its length is the size and its angle the phase. So a 230 V mains supply,[^10] taken as the starting point for angles, is 230∠0°. And resolving a phasor into its two components,[^11] I cos θ and I sin θ, is going back with a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ. **Find the length with Pythagoras and the angle with tan⁻¹(b ÷ a), check the angle against a sketch and turn it 180° when the arrow points left;[^5] go back with a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ.[^8]**

analogy.text: A navigator can give a ship's position from a buoy two ways: 3 km east and 4 km north, or 5 km away on a bearing of 036.87°. It is the same spot, named by parts or by a distance and a direction, as 3 + j4 and 5∠53.13° name the same arrow. The distance comes from Pythagoras and the direction from tan⁻¹, just as here.
analogy.breaks: A bearing is measured clockwise from north, but the angle here is measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis, which points east, so the same direction is 53.13° here, not 36.87°. Bearings also run from 0° to 360°, where this course usually gives angles from just above −180° to 180°.

practice.text:
- Sketch the arrow first: which quarter does its tip land in?
- Find the length: r = √(a² + b²). Square the sizes of the parts, never the j.
- Set the calculator to degrees and work out tan⁻¹(b ÷ a).
- Check it against the sketch. If a is negative, the answer points the wrong way: add 180° when the arrow points up, take 180° away when it points down. Either half turn lands on the arrow; this way keeps the angle between −180° and 180°.
- If the arrow lies on an axis, read the angle off the sketch: 0° right, 90° up, 180° left, −90° down. tan⁻¹ of anything ÷ 0 gives an error.
- Write the answer as r∠θ, then check it by going back: r cos θ and r sin θ should give a and b.

**Rule of thumb:** Top right is 0° to 90°, top left 90° to 180°, bottom left −90° to −180°, bottom right 0° to −90°. If your angle does not point into the quarter you sketched, it is wrong.

**Rule of thumb:** 360° is a whole turn, so adding or taking it away changes nothing. Use it to bring an angle into the usual range: 5∠270° is 5∠−90°.

**Worked example:** −4 − j3. The sketch puts it 4 left and 3 down, in the bottom left. Length: √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5. Calculator: tan⁻¹(−3 ÷ −4) = tan⁻¹(0.75) = 36.87°, which points top right, the wrong way. The arrow points down, so take 180° away: 36.87° − 180° = −143.13°. So −4 − j3 = 5∠−143.13°. Check: 5 cos(−143.13°) = −4 and 5 sin(−143.13°) = −3.

**Common mistakes**
- Squaring the j. √(3² + (j4)²) = √(9 − 16) is no length. The length of 3 + j4 is √(9 + 16) = 5.
- Trusting the calculator in a left-hand quarter. −1 − j1 is not 1.414∠45°, which is 1 + j1; it is 1.414∠−135°.
- Leaving an angle outside the usual range, such as 270°. Take 360° away: −90°.
- Swapping cos and sin. The across part goes with cos, the up part with sin: 10∠−36.87° is 8 − j6, not −6 + j8.
- Writing a negative length. The [[modulus]] is never negative;[^2] point the angle the other way instead.
- A calculator in radians. tan⁻¹(4 ÷ 3) then shows 0.93, not 53.13.

The complex plane, real across and j up, with an example arrow 3 + j4 named two ways: by its parts, a + jb, and by its length and angle, r∠θ.

Parts, a + jb?
Length and angle, r∠θ?

interactive.title: One arrow, two names
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the dashed calculator arrow, tan⁻¹(b ÷ a), pointing exactly opposite the real arrow, and the 180° arc that fixes it, when you drag the tip into a left-hand quarter.

checks.label: The distance of the point from the origin is called the modulus, and the modulus is never negative: for every whole-step tip on the drag screen, the arrow drawn ends at the tip, and the length in its r∠θ name is the distance of the tip from the origin, more than none

Care must be taken when using a calculator to find an inverse tangent that the solution obtained is in the correct quadrant: for every whole-step tip, the dashed ghost (the calculator's answer) lies along the arrow in the right-hand quarters, points exactly the opposite way in the left-hand quarters, where a half turn is drawn to bring it onto the arrow, is absent on the j axis, and the angle named always points into the tip's own quarter

x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ: with the reverse switch on, for every length and every whole-degree angle tried, the arrow ends r cos θ across and r sin θ up, its shadows on the two axes end level with its tip, and the parts named are those two

Known answers worked by hand: 3 + j4 = 5∠53.13°; 6 − j8 is 10 long (14 with the sides added, √−28 with the j squared); 4 + j3 is at 36.87°; for −3 − j4 the calculator says 53.13° and the angle is −126.87°, and the drag screen opens drawing just that; for −3 + j4, −53.13° and 126.87°; −1 − j1 = 1.414∠−135°, and −135° + 360° = 225°; −126.87° + 360° = 233.13°; 5∠270° = 5∠−90° = −j5; 10∠30° = 8.66 + j5 and 10∠150° = −8.66 + j5; 4∠120° = −2 + j3.464; −j5 = 5∠−90° and −4 = 4∠180°; −2 + j1 = 2.236∠153.43°, its ghost at −26.57°; 10∠−36.87° = 8 − j6; −4 − j3 = 5∠−143.13°, which goes back to −4 − j3

Each puzzle takes only its right answer: every answer is worked out from the lesson's rule or from its named slip, the right one matches an independent working (atan2, or cos and sin of the angle in radians), and only it fills in the unknown name; each wrong one is drawn as what its slip makes, marked as a mistake
Before an answer, a puzzle shows only its question: its one arrow and what is given, the unknown name as a question mark, no working, no ghost, no fix and nothing marked as a mistake
Every demonstration finishes within 4.6 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 3 s

From outside the rule: the lesson's fix agrees with the two-argument arctangent (atan2) at every whole-step point from −5 to 5; a navigator 3 km east and 4 km north of a buoy is 5 km away on a bearing of 036.87°, which is 90° − 53.13°; and tan⁻¹(4 ÷ 3) is 0.93 in radians

applied.problem: Swapping cos and sin for 10∠−36.87° gives across 10 sin(−36.87°) = −6 and up 10 cos(−36.87°) = 8, so the slip is −6 + j8, not 6 − j8 (which is 10∠−53.13°).
It says lengths are rounded to two decimal places, but the lesson shows 1.414, 2.236 and 3.464; and no later lesson in this course (i6 to i8) meets a third way of writing r∠θ.

"This course's angles run from just above −180° to 180°" is too absolute: this lesson itself names 5∠270° and 233.13°, and adding angles in the next lesson can go past 180°; the range is the usual choice.
The tip snaps to whole steps and can sit on the j axis, where a is 0 and b ÷ a has no value, so the ghost cannot carry that number or lie anywhere there.

notes.problem: Step 12 slip "cos and sin swapped: across part" is 6, but swapping them for 10∠−36.87° gives 10 sin(−36.87°) = −6 across (and 8 up); the slip answer should be −6 + j8.

"The calculator" here means its tan⁻¹ key; many scientific calculators also have a rectangular-to-polar (Pol) function that gives the angle in the right quarter directly. True as written in context, but could be said once.
